title: Degree
description: Measure relation and result width precisely, distinguish degree from cardinality, and preserve explicit SQL output contracts.
notes:
## Degree counts attributes

The degree of a relation is the number of attributes in its schema. Student(student_id, student_name, programme, score) has degree four because its schema contains four named roles. It does not matter whether the current relation contains one student or ten thousand students. Degree measures the width of each fact's structure rather than the size of the current population.

This definition is simple, but it helps separate several common questions. How many students are recorded asks about tuples. How many properties describe each student asks about attributes. How many distinct programmes occur asks about values in one attribute. These measurements can all be different for the same dataset. State which object is being counted before choosing an SQL aggregate or interpreting a reported number.

## Cardinality is a different measurement

Cardinality counts tuples in a relation instance. A four-attribute Student relation with seven student tuples has degree four and cardinality seven. Deleting two students changes cardinality to five while leaving degree four. Updating a score can change a recorded fact without changing either measurement. A pair of equal measurements does not mean the underlying concepts are interchangeable.

An empty Student relation still has degree four. It has no current tuples, but the schema continues to define their required structure. Treating an empty table as having no columns confuses absent facts with absent definitions. An empty query result likewise retains its output column definitions even though some command-line output formats do not print headers when there are no returned rows.

## Names describe small degrees

A relation of degree one is unary, degree two is binary, and degree three is ternary. More generally, an n-ary relation has n attributes. A unary relation of programme codes can contain many distinct tuples, each with one programme value. Unary does not mean exactly one row, and binary does not mean that its values must be encoded as zero and one.

Use these names only for the number of attributes in this context. A binary relationship in an entity-relationship model can refer to participation of two entity types, which is another use of similar vocabulary. An implementing association table may contain extra attributes such as a date or score. Count its actual schema attributes when determining its relational degree rather than copying a diagram label uncritically.

## Tuple shape follows the schema

Every tuple in a relation has the attributes defined by its schema. A permitted SQL NULL in score does not remove that attribute position. A tuple with three ordinary values and one NULL in a four-column table is still a four-column row. Counting only nonmissing cells would measure recorded values in that row, not the relation's degree.

Similarly, omitting a column from an INSERT target list does not shrink the stored row. A default or permitted absence can supply its value according to the table definition. A prohibited omission can make the write fail. The supplied expression list and the stored row structure are different things, so read the actual schema when explaining degree after an insertion.

## Projection determines a query's output degree

A query selecting student_id and student_name produces an output of degree two. Its source Student table can still have degree four. The selected attributes define the result contract without changing the persistent source structure. A filter changes which rows qualify; it does not by itself change the selected attribute list or its degree.

```sql
SELECT student_id, student_name
FROM students
WHERE active = 1
ORDER BY student_id;
```

Assume the source has additional attributes such as programme and active. This query's output still has two columns. An empty result still has the same logical output degree. DISTINCT would affect repeated output rows rather than remove an attribute. ORDER BY can arrange presentation but does not add the sort expression to the selected result unless it is selected explicitly.

## Expressions create output attributes

A computed expression occupies one output attribute position when selected. SELECT student_id, lecture_hours + lab_hours AS total_hours has degree two, regardless of the fact that the expression reads two source attributes. Count the selected results rather than the number of column references occurring inside their expressions. An alias names a result attribute without adding another one.

An aggregate also produces an output attribute. SELECT COUNT(*) AS student_count without GROUP BY has degree one and ordinarily returns one aggregate row, including a zero count for empty input. The asterisk inside COUNT does not expand into the source columns. This is different from SELECT *, which expands available source columns into separate output attributes under the engine's applicable rules.

## Combined sources need explicit projection

A join can make attributes from several sources available. The number of rows can expand when one source fact has several matches, but output degree still follows the SELECT list. Selecting a student identifier and a course identifier gives degree two even when the join internally reads many descriptive columns and produces numerous enrollment combinations.

Avoid treating every join as automatically having the sum of source degrees. That description fits particular algebraic constructions with suitably distinguished attributes, but SQL projection can select only a subset. A SELECT star expansion and a deliberately chosen output list can have different widths over the same join. Read the query actually being assessed rather than applying one memorized formula to all joined results.

## Structural changes can change degree

Adding a new attribute increases a relation schema's degree by one. Renaming an attribute leaves the count unchanged, and changing its declared type also need not change degree. These operations can still affect compatibility even when degree is preserved. Degree is a useful structural measurement, but it is not a complete description or fingerprint of a schema.

For an added nullable email column with no explicit non-NULL default, existing SQL rows normally expose NULL in that new position under the definition's rules. Other definitions can supply a default or require additional preparation. The important idea is that every row conforms to the resulting column structure; a schema change does not create permanent old-width and new-width rows in the logical table.

## Zero-degree relations belong to theory

Some relational formalisms allow a schema with no attributes. There is exactly one possible zero-attribute tuple: the empty tuple. Under set semantics, a relation over that schema can therefore contain either no tuples or that single tuple. Its degree is zero in both cases, while cardinality distinguishes the two possible states. This construction is different from a unary relation containing NULL.

These theoretical relations are useful in formal reasoning, including truth-like interpretations. They are not a promise that an ordinary MySQL CREATE TABLE statement can define a zero-column table. Keep the formal model separate from product syntax. Most practical exercises should use clearly named output attributes rather than forcing a theoretical edge case into unsupported SQL table definitions.

## Verify the result contract explicitly

A useful fixture can contain repeated names, missing optional values, and no qualifying rows. Check the selected labels and their order as well as the returned values. A query can return the right facts but still violate a consumer contract by adding an unexpected column or reversing two positional fields. Explicit projection prevents an unrelated source-column addition from silently widening a fixed output.

When explaining degree, identify the relation or result being measured, count its attributes, and separately report tuple cardinality if needed. Distinguish source width from output width, selected expressions from referenced inputs, and theoretical constructions from SQL support. This gives a precise way to discuss structure without confusing it with data volume, missing values, join multiplicity, or the amount of work required to execute a query.

questions.question_text: What does the degree of a relation measure?
options: The number of tuples currently stored
The number of attributes in the relation's schema
The number of distinct values in the primary key
questions.explanation: Degree is defined as the count of attributes (columns) in the relation schema.

questions.question_text: What is the degree of Students(id, name, department, gpa)?
options: It depends on the number of rows
questions.explanation: There are 4 attributes (id, name, department, gpa), so the degree is 4.

questions.question_text: A relation with exactly one attribute is called:
questions.explanation: A relation of degree 1 (one attribute) is called unary.

questions.question_text: If Students currently holds 4 rows and later grows to 10,000 rows, what happens to its degree?
options: It grows proportionally with the number of rows
It stays exactly the same, since degree only depends on the schema's attribute count
It doubles every time rows double
questions.explanation: Degree is a schema-level property (attribute count) and is completely unaffected by how many rows exist.

questions.question_text: Which action changes the degree of a relation?
options: Running ALTER TABLE Students ADD COLUMN email varchar(100)
questions.explanation: Adding a new attribute (column) increases the degree by one; row-level operations never change degree.

questions.question_text: Which of the following correctly distinguishes Degree from its closest sibling concept, Cardinality?
options: Degree counts rows; Cardinality counts columns
Degree counts schema attributes; cardinality counts tuples in the current instance
They are the same measurement expressed differently
Degree changes with every INSERT; Cardinality never changes
questions.explanation: Degree remains stable while the attribute list is unchanged; schema evolution can change it.

questions.question_text: After adding a nullable email VARCHAR(100) column with no explicit non-NULL default, how are existing SQL rows represented?
options: They include the new email attribute with NULL under that definition
They automatically get a randomly generated email
The table becomes invalid until every row supplies an email
questions.explanation: The rows follow the new attribute structure; nullability and default rules determine the added value.

questions.question_text: Is a relation of degree 0 (a schema with zero attributes) theoretically valid in relational algebra?
options: No, every relation must have at least one attribute
Yes; some relational formalisms allow zero-attribute relations, separately from ordinary SQL table support
No, degree 0 is only valid for cardinality, not for relations
Yes, but only if cardinality is also 0
questions.explanation: Over an empty heading the set model permits either no tuples or the one empty tuple; ordinary MySQL table syntax is a separate question.

questions.question_text: A four-attribute relation has no tuples. What is its degree?
questions.explanation: The schema still has four attributes.

questions.question_text: SELECT student_id, score + 5 AS adjusted_score has what output degree?
questions.explanation: The expression produces one selected result attribute alongside the identifier.

questions.question_text: Does a NULL value remove an attribute from a SQL row?
options: Only if several rows are NULL
questions.explanation: Absence is not removal of a column definition.

questions.question_text: What does unary mean for a relation?
questions.explanation: Arity counts attributes.

questions.question_text: Does renaming a column necessarily change degree?
options: No; the number of attributes stays the same
Only if the new name is shorter
questions.explanation: A label change is distinct from an attribute-count change.

questions.question_text: What is the degree of SELECT COUNT(*) AS n?
questions.explanation: COUNT produces one output attribute; its asterisk is not projection expansion.

questions.question_text: Why can a joined query have degree two despite reading many columns?
options: Joins always discard all source types
Its SELECT list chooses only two output attributes
questions.explanation: Available source attributes and selected result attributes differ.

questions.question_text: What does DISTINCT change by itself?
options: Duplicate output-row handling, not the selected attribute count
questions.explanation: Duplicate elimination affects cardinality rather than output width.

questions.question_text: Does equal degree prove two schemas are identical?
options: No; names, domains and constraints can differ
questions.explanation: Degree is only one schema measurement.

questions.question_text: How many possible tuples exist over a zero-attribute heading in the stated set formalism?
questions.explanation: The empty tuple is the only combination over no attributes.

questions.question_text: Why use an explicit SELECT list for a fixed consumer contract?
options: It prevents source additions from silently widening the output
questions.explanation: Projection makes output shape explicit.

questions.question_text: A filter leaves no matches. What happens to the query output degree?
options: It remains determined by the selected attributes
questions.explanation: An empty result still has an output structure.

coding_problems.title: Return a two-attribute student result
coding_problems.task: From the five-column source, return exactly student_id and student_name for active students. Preserve repeated names.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE students (student_id INT PRIMARY KEY, student_name VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL, active INT NOT NULL, lecture_hours INT NOT NULL, lab_hours INT NOT NULL);
constraints: Identifiers are unique; active is 0 or 1; hours are nonnegative integers.
edge_cases: Repeated student names must not collapse student identity.
An empty qualifying population still has the requested logical output columns.
hints: A computed expression counts as one output attribute.
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT student_id, student_name FROM students WHERE active = 1 ORDER BY student_id;
coding_problems.explanation: The selected list defines the result degree independently of source width or qualifying row count.

coding_problems.title: Build a precise three-attribute workload result
coding_problems.task: For active students with lecture_hours + lab_hours >= 4, return exactly student_id, student_name AS display_name, and the sum AS total_hours. Sort student_id.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE students (student_id INT PRIMARY KEY, student_name VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL, active INT NOT NULL, lecture_hours INT NOT NULL, lab_hours INT NOT NULL);
constraints: Identifiers are unique; active is 0 or 1; hours are nonnegative integers.
edge_cases: Repeated student names must not collapse student identity.
An empty qualifying population still has the requested logical output columns.
hints: A computed expression counts as one output attribute.
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT student_id, student_name AS display_name, lecture_hours + lab_hours AS total_hours FROM students WHERE active = 1 AND lecture_hours + lab_hours >= 4 ORDER BY student_id;
coding_problems.explanation: The selected list defines the result degree independently of source width or qualifying row count.
